Abimelech (son of Gideon)
uh-BIM-uh-lek
noun (proper, usurper)
From Hebrew Abimelek, "my father is king" (or "the king is my father"), from ab, father, and melek, king; an irony in the mouth of one who made himself king by murder.

📖 Biblical Definition

Abimelech was the son of Gideon by a concubine of Shechem, a man who grasped at a kingship his father had refused and waded to it through the blood of his own house. Persuading the men of Shechem to back him, he hired vain and light fellows, "and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, being threescore and ten persons, upon one stone" (Judg 9:5); only Jotham the youngest escaped, who from mount Gerizim spoke the parable of the bramble king and pronounced a curse. Abimelech reigned three years over Israel by violence, until God sent an evil spirit between him and the men of Shechem, that the cruelty done to Gideon's seventy sons might be requited. So the Scripture renders the verdict plainly: "Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren" (Judg 9:56). As he besieged Thebez, a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon his head and brake his skull; ashamed to die by a woman's hand, he had his armourbearer thrust him through. This dictionary confesses Abimelech a bloody usurper whose tyranny God judged in kind, a standing proof that the LORD repays the wickedness of the proud upon their own heads. (The Philistine kings of Gerar in Genesis 20 and 26 bore the same royal title Abimelech, but are not this man.)

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The son of Gideon who murdered his seventy brethren upon one stone and made himself king at Shechem. God repaid his wickedness, and a woman's cast millstone crushed his skull — tyranny judged in kind.

ABIMELECH, noun. The son of Gideon who slew his seventy brethren and reigned as a usurper-king over Israel at Shechem.

He hired vain men, murdered the sons of Jerubbaal upon one stone, and ruled three years by violence.

"Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren" (Judg 9:56).

His ambition required innocent blood, and the requiting of that blood was the sanction of his fall.

A woman cast a millstone that brake his skull, and he was thrust through by his own armourbearer.

📖 Key Scripture

Judg 9:5 — "And he went unto his father's house at Ophrah, and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, being threescore and ten persons, upon one stone: notwithstanding yet Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left; for he hid himself."

Judg 9:53 — "And a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech's head, and all to brake his skull."

Judg 9:56 — "Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren."

Judg 9:57 — "And all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads: and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Abimelech's tyranny faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that God renders the wickedness of the proud and the murderer upon his own head.

expand to see more

Abimelech is the dark counterpart to his father Gideon, who refused the crown saying the LORD should rule over Israel. The son grasped what the father declined, and built his throne on the bodies of his brethren. His brief reign shows the nature of tyranny seized by blood: it can compel for a season, but it cannot escape the justice of God, who governs even the strife between a usurper and his backers.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the moral government of God over the affairs of men. The text states without flinching that God rendered Abimelech's wickedness upon him and brought upon Shechem the curse of Jotham. The millstone that brake his skull was no accident but the appointed wage of murder. The believer reads here that vengeance belongs to the LORD, who will by no means clear the guilty, and that the ambition which sheds innocent blood ripens to its own destruction.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

His name claims a royal father, yet he won his crown by murdering his father's house, and God repaid the deed in kind.

expand to see more

Abimelek — "my father is king," from ab, father, and melek, king.

He was Gideon's son by a concubine of Shechem, claiming kinship to press his suit for kingship.

He slew the seventy sons of Jerubbaal upon one stone, sparing none but Jotham who hid.

Jotham's parable of the bramble king pronounced the curse that came upon Abimelech and Shechem.

The Philistine kings of Gerar in Gen 20 and 26 bore the same title, but are distinct from Gideon's son.

Usage

"Abimelech slew his seventy brethren upon one stone to make himself king at Shechem."

"God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech upon his own head, as the Scripture plainly says."

"When a woman cast a millstone upon Abimelech's head, the curse of Jotham was fulfilled."
